newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: W.Australia power restrictions remain in place.
newsitem.headline: W.Australia power restrictions remain in place.

text.p: New industrial action by power station controllers will result in the contination of power restrictions for about 700,000 consumers in south-west Western Australia, state-owned Western Power Corp said late on Sunday.

Western Power said in a statement issued less than an hour before it was due to lift power restrictions imposed five days ago in the wake of a strike by 24 of its employees that the restrictions will now have to remain in place because of a decision by about 20 other employees to impose work bans.
"This move is an act of treachery on the people of Western Australia," Western Power managing director David Eiszele said.
"Western Power accepted in good faith guarantees (of a return to work) from trade union leadership," he said.
"As a result of those guarantees, we contacted industry, so that companies that had sustained economic losses as a result of the power dispute could prepare for a full resumption of work," he said.
"We are now assessing the impact there will be on industry and people in their homes as a result of the decision..."

The original strike by 24 coal handlers at Muja Power Station in Collie, about 200 km south west of Perth, was part of a trade union campaign against proposed changes to Western Australia's industrial relations laws.

The coal handlers voted to return to work on Sunday after four hours of hearings in the Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC). The vote prompted Western Power to announce that the power restrictions, which required industry to halt all operations and all other consumers to severely cut back on their power consumption, would be lifted from midnight.
Western Power has increased use of natural gas, distillate and fuel oil as power sources during the strike as well as buying energy from private generators.
Western Power also said it would use the remaining stocks of fuel oil at Muja to warm up the boilers "so that power restrictions can be lifted as soon as possible".

Late on Sunday, however, it said about 20 power station controllers at Muja had voted, a matter of hours after the return to work agreement was reached in the AIRC, to impose bans which effectively destroyed the impact of the agreement.

Earlier on Sunday, a trade union spokesman commenting on the return to work decision said it reflected concern there could have been "inconvenience, serious inconvenience to the public" on Monday if the strike continued.
However, he also warned that other industrial action was pending in relation to the proposed legislative changes.
The disruption to electricity supplies has resulted in thousands of layoffs in industry.
